title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems

A) HIGH-YIELD SUMMARY

  • Neuron: dendrites → soma → axon hillock (summation and firing decision) → axon → terminals. Glia: oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin), Schwann cells (PNS myelin), astrocytes (blood–brain barrier, K⁺ buffering), microglia (immune), ependymal cells (CSF).
  • Action potential: threshold ≈ −55 mV; voltage-gated Na⁺ opens (depolarization) → Na⁺ inactivates + K⁺ opens (repolarization) → hyperpolarization. All-or-none; intensity is coded by firing frequency.
  • Refractory periods: absolute (Na⁺ channels inactivated) and relative (K⁺ still open; stronger stimulus needed).
  • Conduction speed rises with myelin (saltatory, nodes of Ranvier) and larger diameter.
  • Synapse: Ca²⁺ entry triggers vesicle release. Ionotropic receptors are fast; metabotropic (G protein) receptors are slower and longer-lasting. Termination by reuptake, enzymes (acetylcholinesterase) or diffusion.
  • Divisions: CNS (brain, spinal cord) vs. PNS. Somatic (voluntary) vs. autonomic. Sympathetic: thoracolumbar, short pre / long post, NE at target (except sweat glands: ACh). Parasympathetic: craniosacral, long pre / short post, ACh. All preganglionic neurons release ACh onto nicotinic receptors.
  • Reflex arc: receptor → sensory (afferent, dorsal root) → interneuron → motor (efferent, ventral root) → effector.
  • Hormone classes: peptides (water-soluble, membrane receptors, second messengers, fast); steroids (lipid-soluble, intracellular receptors, change transcription, slow); amines (thyroid hormones act like steroids; catecholamines act like peptides).
  • Axes: hypothalamus → anterior pituitary (portal system) for TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, GH, prolactin. Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamus.
  • Feedback: most axes use negative feedback; oxytocin in labor and the LH surge are positive feedback.
  • Key hormones: insulin (β cells, ↓ glucose), glucagon (α cells, ↑ glucose), cortisol (↑ glucose, immunosuppression), aldosterone (Na⁺ reabsorption, K⁺ secretion), PTH (↑ Ca²⁺), calcitonin (↓ Ca²⁺), T₃/T₄ (↑ metabolic rate), epinephrine (fight or flight).

C) COMMON TRAPS + 3 MCAT-STYLE Qs

Trap 1: "The Na⁺/K⁺ pump repolarizes the neuron." Repolarization is due to K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated channels. The pump maintains gradients over the long run; it is too slow to shape a single spike.

Trap 2: Exogenous steroids raise ACTH. Giving glucocorticoids suppresses CRH and ACTH by negative feedback, so the adrenal cortex atrophies. Stopping them suddenly causes adrenal insufficiency.

Q1. A toxin blocks voltage-gated K⁺ channels in a neuron. Which change in the action potential is most likely?

  • A) It fails to reach threshold
  • B) Its repolarization is prolonged
  • C) Its peak amplitude falls to −20 mV
  • D) The resting potential becomes more negative

Answer: B. Without voltage-gated K⁺ efflux, repolarization depends on slower mechanisms, so the spike is wider.

  • A is wrong: reaching threshold depends on Na⁺ channels.
  • B is correct: K⁺ channels drive repolarization.
  • C is wrong: peak amplitude is set by Na⁺ influx (toward E_Na).
  • D is wrong: resting potential is set mostly by K⁺ leak channels, which are not voltage-gated; blocking K⁺ channels would, if anything, depolarize rest.

Q2. A patient has high cortisol and low ACTH. Where is the primary problem most likely located?

  • A) Anterior pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH
  • B) Adrenal tumor secreting cortisol
  • C) Hypothalamic CRH deficiency
  • D) Ectopic ACTH from a lung tumor

Answer: B. Autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH by negative feedback.

  • A is wrong: a pituitary source would raise ACTH.
  • B is correct: high hormone + low upstream signal points to the gland itself.
  • C is wrong: CRH deficiency would lower both ACTH and cortisol.
  • D is wrong: ectopic ACTH would raise ACTH.

Q3. A drug blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at autonomic ganglia. Which effect on the heart is expected at rest, when parasympathetic tone dominates?

  • A) Heart rate falls
  • B) Heart rate rises
  • C) No change, because the heart uses muscarinic receptors
  • D) Heart stops

Answer: B. Ganglionic blockade cuts both divisions; removing the dominant vagal (parasympathetic) brake raises heart rate toward the SA node's intrinsic rate (≈ 100 beats/min).

  • A is wrong: the sympathetic input is also blocked, but at rest the larger loss is vagal tone.
  • B is correct: loss of dominant parasympathetic tone.
  • C is wrong: the heart's muscarinic receptors are postganglionic; the drug blocks the ganglion upstream.
  • D is wrong: the SA node is autorhythmic and keeps firing without autonomic input.
